Murder by Georgia Regulators.
Columbus, Ga., June 7.—For some time considerable excitement has been caused in Haywood district, Chattooga county, from the fact that Allen Chapmen, a colored man, wss living and co-habiting with a very comely girl of pure white blood.

Warnings had been sent to both of them in an anonymous way several times, that if they continued to inhabit the same cabin there would be trouble.

These warnings were not heeded, and ominous mutterings of a disturbance began to fill the air. Last night a band of men, masked and armed, made their appearance at his door and demanded the girl. In her place Chapman, the colored man, presented himself with a shot gun, The crowd at once opened fire upon him. flicking his body full of shot and retreated. Chapman was horribly wounded, and is now reported dead.

A Job that was Finished by Murder. ALBANY, Feb. 19.—A murder occured at Hope Falls, Hamilton County, this morning, which has created much excitement in that section. Edward Earl, a farmer, was some four years ago convicted of an assault on his wife, and, after trial, was sent to Dannemora prison, from which he was recently released. His punishment, however, worked no reformation, and he is said to have deceived, time and again, that he would finish the job. This morning, when the woman went to the barn to feed some cattle, Earl jumped out from a corner in which he was secreted and stabbed her through the heart. The woman died instantly. Earl went to the nearest con-stable and asked to be taken into custody, that he might not injure his wife. Search was then made, and the woman was found dead. The deed was committed with an knife stolen from a nearby tannery, where Earl was seen grinding it a day or two ago. ONE MURDER AND ELEVEN LYNCHINGS. Negroes Taken from Jail and Hung while their Trial was in Progress.
SPRINGFIELD, Tenn., Feb. 19.—On the night of Sept. 8 last a farmer named Laprade was murdered. He lived alone, in the neighborhood of Sadlersville, Robinson County, and was supposed to have a hoard of money. A party of negroes went to his house, and tortured him horribly to make him confess where the money was concealed, which he protested he did not have. He was burned with torches, cut with knives, and strung up by the neck repeatedly. Finally his skull was crushed in with an axe, and the body thrown into a sink hole.

The murder caused intense excitement. An old negro named James Higgins was suspected of having been concerned in it. He was arrested and made statements inculpating other negroes. A party of lynchers took him out and roasted his feet until he made a full confession. Higgins had to have one of his feet amputated, and subsequently died in jail.

On the night of Sept. 15 two others of those who had been arrested on charge of the murder, Bell and Jamieson, were taken from jail and lynched, and at the same time a white man named Ramsey was shot to death in his cell. He was awaiting trial for shooting a Miss Holt because she had rejected him for another suitor.

After these events the excitement quieted down, and it looked as if the regular course of justice would not be interfered with in the case of the remaining prisoners. The lynching feeling was, however, revived by the report that the accused were to be granted a change of venue. On the night of the 14th inst. a party of mounted men rode into town and made for the jail. They had broken in the door when Judge Stork and Attorney-General Bell arrived and addressed the mob, urging them to refrain from lawless behavior, and pledging them that the prisoners should be punished to the full extent of the law if found guilty. The Attorney-General assured them that he would conduct the prosecution with the greatest possible energy.

The lynchers seemed to be satisfied by these assurances and dispersed; but it was thought best to have a company of State troops in attendance when the trial began. Two of the accused, Bill Murphy and Anthony Duffy, testified for the State. They were released last Thursday, and immediately returned to their former haunts. This stirred up the lynch-law feeling again.

The militia company gave a parade in the Court House yard before dark last night. After dark a furious thunder storm set in, and fear of lynching the prisoners vanished. A night session of the court was held to finish the trial, and Judge Stark gave his charge to the jury, after which the Sheriff proceeded with the prisoners—James Higgins, Lock Mallory, Lon. Thiveat, Robert Thiveat, and James Elder—to the jail. A mob of about two hundred pressed upon the Sheriff, took the prisoners, cleared the Court House and grounds, stationed a strong picket guard around them, and hung them from the second-story windows of the Court House.

The onset of the mob was so sudden and boisterous, accompanied by firing of pistols and guns into the air, as to terrify the spectators in the court room, who jumped from the windows and hastened from the scene. The lynchers numbered 200 well-armed men, who came in from three directions on horseback, and dispersed in the same manner. They did not shoot or mutilate the prisoners, but left them hanging until assured that they were dead. They announced that they were going to pursue and lynch the two negroes who had been released. NASHVILLE, Tenn., Feb. 19.—It is reported that Duffy and Murphy, the Laprade murderers, who turned State's evidence, were found hanging to a tree near Guthrie, Ky., this morning.

RAGIC MIDNIGHT SCENE IN WINCHES
A TRAGIC MIDNIGHT SCENE IN WINCHESTER, TENN. — TROOPS ASSEMBLE TO PROTECT THE FIVE NEGROES BEING TRIED FOR THE MURDER OF LAPRADE — THE PRISONERS ARE CAPTURED BY A MOB OF TWO HUNDRED MEN AND HUNG FROM THE SECOND-STORY WINDOWS OF THE JOURT-HOUSE.

CINCINNATI, February 19 — Telegrams from Winchester, Tenn., represent that troops were present for the protection of the alleged Laprade murderers on trial there, and that they gave a parade in the court-house yesterday before dark; that after dark a furious thunder-storm came on, and all fear of the prisoners being lynched then vanished. A night session was held to finish the trial. Judge Stark gave his charge to the jury; after which the sheriff proceeded with the prisoners, James Higgins, Jack Mallory, Lon Thweat, Robert Thweat, and James Elder, to jail. A mob or about two hundred pressed upon the sheriff, took the prisoners, closed the court-house and its grounds, stationed a strong picket-guard around them, and hung the five negro prisoners from the second-story windows of the court-house. The onset of the mob was from without, and was so sudden and boisterous, accompanied by the firing of pistols and guns into the air, as to terrify the spectators in the court-room, who jumped from the windows and hastened from the scene. Murphy and Duffy, charged with complicity in the murder, having been released on Thursday, had returned to their old stamping-ground, which is thought to have precipitated the action of the mob. The mob are after them, and it is believed they will be lynched not later than tonight. The mob numbered two hundred well-armed men, who came in from four directions on horseback, and dispersed in the same manner. They did not shoot or mutilate their prisoners, but left them hanging when assured they were dead. The dispatches are silent as to what the military were doing all this while.

Painfully Personal. A Strange Scene in the Virginia Court of Appeals. In a recent application before the court of appeals of Virginia for a rehearing in an important insurance case, Mr. John Howard, a prominent lawyer of Richmond, stated that the president of the court (Chief Justice R. C. L Moncurel) is mentally so feeble and pecuniarily so interested in the result of the suit "that his bare presence on the bench renders the decision infected and vitiated with illegality," and he wished it understood that no such decision would or could be regarded or recognized by his clients. This has elicited a severe rejoinder from a unanimous court, Judge Moncure not sitting. It is shown by Mr. Howard's own associate counsel and his client that Mr. Howard insisted on Judge Moncure sitting in the case, and that he expressed an unwillingness to proceed with the case unless Judge Moncure would sit. The court pays a glowing tribute to the judge's devotion to duty and impartial administra-
tion of justice, and adds that "this is not the first time Mr. John Howard has grossly offended against all propriety in his demeanor to the court." Mr. Howard, in a note to the court, asked permission to withdraw the whole of the argument, with the privilege of making a revision, and disclaiming any intention that any construction should be placed upon it "incompatible with that high personal and professional respect for the court and each of the judges which it has ever been his pleasure to feel and purpose to show." The court granted Mr. Howard's request, adding, "And in view of Mr. Howard's expressed disclaimer and the withdrawal of the whole of his offensive matter the court forbears to take any further action." Mr. Howard then addressed the court, concluding with the remark "that the true inquiry was not who made the suggestion as to the incompetency of the judge, or whether it should not have been sooner made, but whether in December last, when he rendered the decision, he was not mentally incapable of understanding and deciding so great a litigation, and whether he was not personally so situated in respect to it as to unfit him to act as a judge—inquiries which could not be escaped by making a personal issue with himself."

Seven Negroes Lynched.

Five Hanged on the Front of a Tennessee Court House and Two in the Woods. Springfield, Tenn., dispatch to N. Y. World.

The country is in a fever-heat of excitement over the wholesale lynching which occurred Friday night. The tragedy which culminated in the lynching of the five negroes implicated in the murder of Mr. Laprade, makes a total of ten deaths which have thus far resulted from the fearful butchery. The crime for which these negroes were lynched was the murder of a farmer named Laprade, who lived alone near Sadlersville, Robinson county, about a mile away from any neighbor. The report was current that he and his two brothers had fallen heirs to $9,000 a few days before the murder. A party of nine negroes went to his house on the night of September 8, 1880. Going in the rear of his dwelling, one of them knocked at the door, and imitating the voice of Laprade's brother, asked for admission. Laprade opened the door without thought of harm. They met the sheriff at the court-room door, with presented pistols, took the prisoners from him and ordered the lights all out. They then carried all five of the negroes to the east door of the court-house, where ropes were awaiting them, and they were drawn up by willing hands in the veranda above.

They all died without a struggle, except Jim Elder, who had to be thrown down, tied and then raised. Hundreds of shots were fired, but none at the prisoners.

The mob guarded the bodies until they were sure they were dead, and the leader gave the order, "disperse my men, to your homes," and they immediately departed, going in three directions.

They came in on horses, but went to the conrt-house, on foot and were not discovered till they met the prisoners at the door.

It is thought that the cause of this trouble to-night, was the releasing of Bill Murphy and Anthony Duffy, at 12 o'clock last night. When released they went right back into the vicinity where they had committed their terrible crime and were seen there to-day. The people, fearing the prisoners would appeal from the verdict of the jury, and then, if the case was sent back, the state would have no witnesses, and determined there should be no escape for, beyond a doubt, they were guilty. This is the verdict of every citizen who heard the testimony.

The Stokers and Chargers Refuse to Work with Negroes and Strike—Their Places Filled with Negroes.

There has been a little trouble at the Gas Works during this week occasioned by the refusal of certain Hibernians who have been employed there as stokers and chargers, to work with a colored man who was employed by Superintendent Dillon as a fireman. Tuesday the colored man was employed and Wednesday evening when the night turn was about to go to work the whole party rebelled and said none of them would go to work unless the negro was discontinued. It was too late to do anything and so Superintendent Dillon acceded to their demands for the time. During the evening he summoned the Trustees of the Works and they ratified his action in hiring the colored man, and yesterday he was sent to work again. In the evening, when the night turn came to go to work again the performance of the preceding evening was repeated, but this time unsuccessfully, as a large number of negroes was at once set to work in the places of the strikers.

Secretary Harry Caldwell went out to the works at the time of the strike in the evening and remained several hours, superintending and assisting when necessary.

An Intelligencer commissioner was at the works at ten o'clock last night and found everything quiet and all working smoothly. Mr. Dillon was supervising the manufacture of gas, and said that the new hands were doing nearly as well as the old ones. There had been 14 men at work, nearly all of whom had quit. He had put to work in their places ten negroes, and proposed to keep them there. In the first place there had been only one negro employed, and he had hired him as a fireman merely to relieve the stokers and chargers of some of their arduous labors. One man had already come back and asked to go to work again, but he had refused them permission, and so far as he was concerned he did not intend to take any of them back.

A Statement From Superintendent Dilion as to the Recent Difficulty. Editors Intelligencer.
A Statement From Superintendent Dillion as to the Recent Difficulty.
Editors Intelligencer.

There has been a good deal of talk about my management of the Gas Works for the past few weeks, especially in regard to the employment of some colored men as firemen, and I had intended to let the whole story, as told by the discharged men in the Register, go for what it would bring, trusting that my life for the past fifty-two years in the city had been so spent that no one knew me would believe that I would be guilty of an act of injustice to any man, especially a laboring man, as I have been identified with laboring men all my life. But from a card in your paper a day or two ago, and also from private information, I have learned that an effort is being made to displace me and restore my predecessor, on the ground that I have been unjust in my treatment of white men at the Gas Works. A true statement of my conduct will, I hope, disabuse the minds of all persons, who are willing to be convinced, of any intention on my part to wrong ony man.

The day before Christmas I was waited on by the men in a body, who told me that unless I would employ two more men in each turn, making four in all, that they would stop working in twelve hours. This meant that Christmas day would be made a day of darkness for this city, and I had but one course to follow and that was to submit with as good a grace as I could and give them the men. There was a remarkable fact in connection with this strike, and it was that the man who seemed to be the leader based his demand on the ground that in 1873, the same number of men I then had, made but 73,000 feet of gas on a turn, and that they were now making 120,000 feet in the same time. How could he have carried this record of the gas made in his mind for more than seven years? The idea is absurd. But one man in this city had that knowledge, and he is the one who hoped to be benefitted

by my downfall if that strike had been a success in bringing me into disgrace. About a week after this occurrence I put out the fires in the small retort house, not having any further use for that house, and of course did not need so many men. In reducing the force I did as any other prudent man would have done, i.e., I quietly dropped the men, who were the leaders in the above strike.

I changed the charges from six hours to four, and in so doing necessarily increased the labor of the men, and in order to assist them in their labor I employed two colored men, who had been for years firemen on the river, believing them to be thoroughly qualified for that work. They were not put in any white men's places. No man was discharged to make a place for them. The men who claimed they were discharged for that purpose do not tell the truth, for they were entirely new men, who were an addition to the force, and not put in to fill any vacancies.

The white men waited on me the first day the colored men came to work, and notified me that they would not work if the "niggers" were not discharged and two white men put in their places. Again I had to submit. But the next day I questioned each man, and was pointedly informed that they would quit unless I would promise not to employ any "niggers." This being the second strike, and being satisfied that if I was driven by the men to accedeing to their demands that my usefulness as Superintendent was at an end, I employed nine colored men, who, with two or three white men who saw fit to stay, now compose the force employed at the works.

I was much surprised at the majority of the strikers making this last demand, as one of them had worked as a bricklayer with colored men for several years, another worked in the same shop with a colored man, and another had worked last summer at the works for several months in digging the hole for the new tank with nine colored men. Three of them had marched last summer in Republican processions with colored men. Another was an unnaturalized Englishman, and but four of them were known to me to be dyed in-the-wool Democrats.

The insinuation that any man was ever intimidated by me as to his manner of voting or that I ever proscribed any man for his religious belief is untrue. The very man who makes this charge against me was discharged by my predecessor, who is of his own creed and politics, and was restored by me to the place he formerly held at the Works.

Hoping that this hurried statement may at least show the public that I have intentionally wronged no man I take my leave of the matter. J. M. Dillon.
gas-works-strike-wheeling-1881-01-12.A6:
THE GAS WORKS. More Matter on the Subject of the Strike.
I beg space in the REGISTER for a word of reply to the very remarkable card of Mr. J. M. Dillon in this morning's (Thursday's) Intelligencer. The card is remarkable in appearing at this particular time—the morning of election day—as well as in its statements, and the impression they are evidently intended to make.

The writer of this is too much interested in earning a livelihood for himself and his family, in any honest way, to make himself a party to any quarrel there may be between Mr. Dillon and Mr. Brown, the late Superintendent, and he presumes the latter is able to take care of his own interests. All I wish to do now is to correct some of Mr. Dillon's statements, especially so far as they concern myself.

It is true, I made the statement as to the amount of gas made in 1873, and at present, by the same number of men, but I can assure Mr. Dillon that it was made on my own knowledge and recollection, and not on any information derived from Mr. Brown, with whom I had no conversation on the subject. It is true that I was at one time discharged by Mr. Brown, late superintendent; but he did what Mr. Dillon has not yet done, unless possibly by this card of his—he informed me of the cause. I do not know what Mr. Dillon may understand by intimidation. I do know he never intimidated me; but I also know that he on many occasions intimated to his workmen his political preferences.

A careful reading of his card will show that Mr. Dillon's statements are contradictory. If he put out the fires in the small retort house, "quietly dropped some men" and then hired two colored men, were they not "put in some white men's places?" Were they not put in the places of the men discharged? Mr. Dillon had better try another card, and devetail his statement at title better. It is true Mr. Dillon stopped the fires in the small retort house. Will he tell us why he has lighted them again? It would be easier, perhaps, to do that than to explain how he discharged the men, put out those fires, relit the fires and then employed the two negroes, who were "not put in the place of any white men," as he says.

The truth is, and! Mr. Dillon's own card is full proof, that his whole action in the matter was for the purpose of forcing the men to quit, or put themselves in such a position that he could find some pretence plausible to the general public unacquainted with the real facts to discharge men in order to make places for others.

Mr. Dillon also says he discharged the leaders of the strike. Let me ask him, is it not the fact that the real leader, the man who was most active and outspoken in the strike, is still in his place at the works? How is it Mr. Dillon—is not this true? And can you tell the public why?

In conclusion, I have no wish to say anything to the injury of Mr. Dillon, or indeed of any man; but when any man seeks to put me and my fellow workmen in a false position before the public, I shall do my best to correct it.

Respectfully, &c.

JOHN FLAHEKTY.

A CARD
A CARD
From the Late Superintendent of the Gas Works.
Editors Intelligencer.

In the statement over the signature of I. M. Dillon, that appeared in the Intelligencer of the 27th inst., it is intimated in unmistakable terms that I have in some way been instrumental in causing the recent trouble amongst the employes at the Gas Works, arising from the employment of colored men to the exclusion of the white workmen. Mr. Dillon says that "I hoped to be benefitted by his downfall, if that strike had been a success in bringing him into dicgrace." I respectfully, and as a matter of justice, ask to be allowed space for a few remarks in reply to his unwarranted assertions.

Most of those white men are strangers to me. I know two of them, but I can say, and am prepared to substantiate it in the most solemn manner, that while these men were employed at the Gas Works under Mr. Dillon I have had no conversation with them directly or indirectly on the subject of the "strike." I have had nothing to do with it. Can Mr. Dillon show that I had? Can he show that I have ever tried to influence any of his employes to his disadvantage? Or has this card of his appeared merely because it was deemed appropriate for the morning of a city election?

Mr. Dillon takes occasion to mention my "creed and politics." He might do better if, instead of occupying his mind with other men's "creed and politics," he would devote his leisure hours to studying the duties of his new position, and acquiring a better knowledge of them.

I can conscientiously say that while I was at the Gas works I have never been influenced by either creed or politics in my official intercourse with the men employed there. But since it has been Mr. Dillon's pleasure to speak of other men's "creed and politics," I may, I hope, be excused if I inquire, was it not on account of their "creed and politics" that soon after I quit the Gas works some ten or twelve skilled and experienced men employed were discharged. There was no fault alleged against them. Two of them, on the contrary, hold excellent testimonials as to good conduct and efficiency, signed by Mr. Dillon himself a day or two after they were discharged. How can this be explained?

I have never desired any controversy with Mr. Dillon. We have always, during my residence of fourteen years in this city, been, as I thought, on good terms, and therefore I have suffered to pass unnoticed many statements to my disadvantage that have from time to time appeared in the columns of the INTELLIGENCE, as the substance of interviews of a local reporter with Mr. Dillon. For instance—the apparatus was defective, and Mr. Dillon had to improve it; he obtained a larger return of gas from the coal than I had done, etc. The carbonizing account kept by me would refute this, and show the reverse to have been the case. Mr. Dillon avoids mentioning the quality of the gas made in my time. How does the gas supplied to the citizens of Wheeling, particularly this winter, compare both in quality and quantity with the gas made previous to his superior management?

In this connection I would ask attention to one or two matters illustrative of the present able management. Towards the fall of 1879 I recommended the erection of three benches or ovens of five retorts each in the place of four old dilapidated ones of three retorts each, that had been in use about 30 years, and the city Council adopted my plan in preference to a proposition to build a new gas holder at that late period of the year. Those old retorts could not be relied on and additional gas holders would not avail without the means for making gas. The result proved that that plan was the right one, for the apparatus, thus enlarged, was more than sufficient for the supply of the increased demand for gas in the winter of that year. I have said it was more than sufficient, because one of those three benches of "fives" was not started or put into use that winter. The producing capacity of its five retorts was about thirty thousand (30,000) cubic feet of gas daily.

This being the case why was it stated in a report made last June to the Council that "during the last holiday season the works were as severely taxed as they could stand. Two other negroes were in close pursuit, whom Turner was keeping at a distance by threatening them with a long stick, the only weapon he has carried since committing the deed. Batty met him and presented a musket in his face, and he surrendered promptly. He was identified by parties in the neighborhood, and brought here on the 5.30 tram, this evening, and lodged in jail. Turner is a slender-build, copper-colored negro, and says he is nineteen years old. He committed the deed on the 8th inst., since which time different parties have been in pursuit of him every day, and he has been seen by some one who knew him almost every day. He has not been exceeding fifteen miles from Murfreesboro during the time, and whenever seen, did not seem to be making any special effort to conceal himself, but always managed to evade his pursuers. On the 14th he was arrested by parties near Eagleville, but escaped. On Saturday last he was chased and fired at several times, but escaped. Davis, and said he had never been in the neighborhood where the crime was committed. The last Legislature passed a law to
take the sense of the people of the State as to the necessity of calling a Convention to revise the Constitution, and accordingly the question will be voted on at the August election. Article XII of the Constitution as it stands provides that, when a majority of the members of the two Houses of the Legislature within the first twenty days of the session, concur, they may pass a law to take the sense of the people as to the necessity of calling a Convention. The question shall be submitted to the people at the next general election, and if a majority of all the voters of the State vote therefor, at the next meeting of the Legislature the question shall a second time be submitted to the people, and if a majority of the voters favor the proposition, the Legislature must call a Constitutional Convention.

This section renders it almost an impossibility to ever change the document, and its makers were thus particular with reference to a change so that no interference could be made in regard to slavery, much feared at the time. That institution having been abolished, all laws in reference to it have become dead letters, while a change in the times has rendered many other of the articles void and inoperative. That there is a necessity for a revision no thinking man will deny, and, this being the case, it becomes the people to turn out en masse and vote to call a Convention. The question has been put to the people several times, but owing to the failure of the masses to understand or to care whether a change is made or not, the necessary majority of all the voters in the State has never been obtained. We fear a like result will follow the coming effort to get a majority. The people have it in their power to vote on either side of the question, and if they fail to vote at all it is hardly fair that it should be taken that they are opposed to the change. Every effort should be made to poll as large a vote as possible, but if it is largely in favor of calling the Convention and does not reach the necessary majority, it should become the duty of the next Legislature to take revolutionary measures toward a change, by appointing the time and place for holding a Convention and asking the people to send delegates to it. The duty of such a Convention would be to make the needed changes in the Constitution, and it would then remain for the people to adopt or reject it at the polls. We wish that every voter could be made to understand the importance of his vote in the matter, and we suggest that officers of the election take special pains to ask each man to vote on the question.

It really does seem that the country is experiencing the evil effects of a moral collapse of unexampled character. Not a week, a day—nay, an hour—passes by without some revelation of a desperate crime being made. No section of the country is free from lawless deeds; no class of society is exempt from the presence of the crimson stains of violence. Thoughtful people are roused by the number and startling character of the crimes which are being committed everywhere. The germs of the epidemic seem to pervade the whole moral atmosphere; corrupting, enraging and nerving the victims of the disorder to deeds of death. The crime craze has reached the higher social circles, and all sorts of scandals and peccadillos result therefrom. Indeed, among the high and the low, the rich and the poor, the learned and the unlearned, there seems to have been a complete letting down of moral principle; and instead of peace and safety, a reign of crime has been inaugurated. The records of a single day's development of crime would fill a volume. To day, a negro in Louisiana attempts a dastardly outrage on a young lady; to morrow morning's sun will greet a ghastly corpse swinging to the limb of a tree. A jail guard in Arkansas opens the door of the prison and allows a quartette of dangerous desperadoes to go their way. In another part of the same State, a howling mob takes from the jail a prisoner under a long sentence, shoot, and then hang him. In Rutherford county, Tennessee, a negro man, for a brutal outrage, is seized by a mob of lynchers, and speedily dispatched. Two murders and one legal execution took place in Arkansas last Friday, and on the same day two men were killed in affrays, one hanged by the officers of the law in Henry county, Missouri, while at Maryville, in the same State, two youths, convicted of the crime of killing their own father, were put to death by the Sheriff in accordance with the sentence of a court. In Texas several persons were wounded and bruised in affrays, and some were killed outright on this same fatal Friday. We read of Italian bandits domiciled in New Orleans, and the next instant our eyes behold the bloody records of American brigands, who stopped a whole train, killed the conductor and a passenger, and carried away the contents of the express safe. But we have no disposition to extend the list further. It is a sickening record. The crimes include every variety and grade. Crime against life, against property, against virtue, against morality; the violent struggle of infuriated men, the stealthy shot of the concealed assassins; the pitiless embrace of the lusty brute; the invasion of the sanctities of home; slanders and lapses of every grade and character constitute a part of the records of the crimes of a week.

What can be the matter? Is the moral world out of joint? May there not be some subtle influence—some atmospheric conditions that act upon the cerebral organs to produce a species of madness? Whether that be the case or not, certain it is that the country seems to be afflicted with an epidemic of crime, such as his never before swept over it. The moral tone of the people and the press appear to be low. Mob law is justified and defended by public prints, and deeds of violence seem to excite but a passing consideration. Something must be done to check the reign of lawlessness. What is the cause? No remedy can be applied without a knowledge of the nature of the disease.

Francisco Alamilla, a Mexican political leader, lying in jail at Humarguillo, was shot without judge or trial.

The bodies of Periander Pollock and wife, keepers of the toll house at Six Mile Canon. near Virginia City, Nev., were found in the charred ruins of their house on the night of the 28th ult. The heads of both were crushed. A case of murder.

J. Dundom has been lodged in jail at Deadwood, charged with the murder of his wife on Christmas.

A srtanger pretending to be deaf and dumb, stopping at Mrs. B. Munroe's boarding house at East Dalhousie, N. B., fatally shot the landlady's son and daughter, aged 19 and 12 respectively.

John Roberts, of Mount Vernon, O., shot his brother John twice through the body on the 29th ult. The injured man is in a critical condition.

A young farmer named Gray interfered with a negro dance at Round Oak, near Macon, Ga., on the 26th ult., and was fatally stabbed. Gray fired into the assemblage, killing three brothors—Bob, Henry and Dick Jackson—and then crawled out of the house to die.

In a saloon quarrel at Butte, Montana, Joe Campbell mortally wounded Joe Rowells, of Bodie, Col.

Leon Moore, clerk in a store at Boston, Mass., spent Christmas at his home in Biddeford, Me. On the 28th he called on his afflianced, Miss Belle Cushman, an estimable lady, and shot her dead. He then put a bullet through his own head and expired. They were both 21 years of age and belonged to respected families.

A terrible tragedy occurred on the 28th ult., at Bellefonte, Ala., a small station forty-four miles from Chattanooga, resulting in the probably fatal shooting of W. D. Martin, his son John, and C. M. Fennel. They are the only merchants in the place, and the difficulty originated through jealousy. They used pistols.

In a street fight at Eufala, Indian Territory, on the 26th, a carpenter named Ware killed a young man named Grayson. A railway section hand who witnessed the affair became frightened and ran. He was ordered to halt by the police, but refused to comply and was shot dead.

Ole Thompson, a wealthy Norwegian farmer, was found murdered on the farm of his son-in-law on the 27th. The body was horribly mangled. The nephew of the murdered man has disappeared and is supposed to be the murderer.

On the night of the 23d inst., villians entered the Gibbons homestead near Ashland, Kentucky, during the absence of the old folks, and overpowered young Robert Gibbons, Miss Emma Thomas, aged 17 and a 14-year-old daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Gibbons. After outraging the young ladies, the fiends killed all three of their victims, saturated their clothing with oil and fired the premises. The house was consumed completely. The three bodies were recovered horribly mutilated, the heads having been split with a hatchet. A reward of $1,000 is offered for the arrest of the miscreants.

In a shooting affray at Helenwood, Tenn., on the 25th inst., John Cecil was killed and three brothers named West, W. Smith and a man named Thomson were probably fatally injured.

In a quarrel at Knoxville, Tenn., on the evening of the 24th, the youngest son of Gen. Joseph A. Mabry, was killed by Don Lisby.

The Christmas holidays was marked by the usual amount of crime in all directions. One notable feature of that crime was the number of rows and affrays among gangs of workmen. One man was killed and another fatally injured in a bloody row among railroad workmen, at Tampico, O. During a riot among railroad laborers, near Newburgh, N. Y., Sunday, two men were killed; a militia company was called out to quell the disturbance. A workingmen's row near Jeffersonville, Ind., Christmas eve, resulted in the killing of a negro named Mitchell. A Christmas fight among railroad section tenders, near Louisville, Ky., ended with the death of one man. Four Italians were stabbed in an affray in a New York tenement house. One died and the others are in a precarious condition.

D. C. H. Rosenhauer, a prominent physician, was assassinated near Texarkana, Ark., on Christmas eve. A Chinese laundryman is suspected.

South and West.
An explosion which occurred at West Point, Va., on board the steamer West Point, plying between that place and Baltimore, resulted in the total destruction of the boat and the loss of twenty lives. The hands were engaged in discharging the cargo, and after they had been employed nearly two hours unloading, a terrific, yet unexplained explosion, occurred near the forward hatch of the steamer, and almost instantly the forward part of the vessel was enveloped in flames. There were sixteen colored men in the forward hold at the time, all of whom were either killed by the explosion or burned to death. Five other men were aft stowing cotton. These jumped overboard, and four of them were drowned. When it was found that there was no hope of saving the steamer she was cut loose from the wharf and the tide carried her two miles up the Panaunkey river, where she continued to burn until everything combustible was destroyed, and her iron hull was broken in two amidships. The steamer was built at Baltimore at a cost of $70,000, and this was her second trip.

At a negro dance in Jones county, Georgia, John W. Gray, a young white planter, got into an altercation with three colored brothers named Jackson, and was fatally stabbed by them. Gray fired into the brothers, killing all three.

The failure of the bank of Haskell, Harris & Co., of Hillaboro, Ill., caused great excitement there. The liabilities are $120,000, assets unknown. One of the directors, W. A. Young, was arrested on a charge of embezzlement as he was about to leave for New Mexico.

SMALLFOX is raging with great severity in some parts of Dakota.

Twelve prisoners, including three awaiting execution, escaped from the jail at Shreveport, La.

JOEL JOHNSON was shot and badly wounded by a negro in Baldwin county, Alabama. His brother Abe, as sheriff, in attempting to arrest the assailant, mortally wounded him, and was himself shot dead.

A FRAGAS at Bellefonte, Ala., resulted in the probably fatal shooting of C. M. Fennel, W. D. Martin and his son John. They were the only merchants in the place, and the difficulty originated in jealousy.

DURING 1881 thirty-six homicides and eighty-two suicides were committed in St. Louis.

GOTHLIEB ENGEL, a prominent young lawyer of Milwaukee, Wis., embezzled, forged, and then absconded.

MRS. CRUZ, living at Florence, Los Angeles county, Cal., was delivered a few days since of six perfectly-formed female children.

WILLIAM H. ERB was hanged at St. Louis for the murder of his wife. On the same day, at Charleston, S. C., Gabriel White (colored) suffered death on the gallows for murdering another colored man.

BETWEEN thirty and forty medical students at Keokuk Iowa, have been stricken down with smallpox, caught from a subject in the dissecting-room that had died of the dread disease. Smallpox also prevails in about forty different places in Illinois.

LAST winter the Dakota legislature organized a new county called Douglass, acting upon affidavits as to its population and property which are now shown to be false. The county has but forty voters, and its taxable property is only about $12,000; but a few of its enterprising citizens, after electing themselves to the county offices, have issued $200,000 in bonds and sent them to New York for a market.

COLONEL L. M. BELL, a prominent planter who lived near Hamburg, Ark., is said to have so brutally beaten and abused his wife an intelligent and refined lady, that she died the other day. Her cruel death so excited the neighborhood that a crowd the next night took Bell from his home and hanged him to a tree.

San Antonio, May 13.—A letter from Kerrville says last Sunday, as Deputy Sheriff Clemens, of Kerrville county, was returning from San Antonio with two prisoners, John Potter and William Dunman, he was waylaid by a party of unknown men near Kerrville and both prisoners taken from him. The men stopped in the middle of the road with drawn revolvers. The deputy could do nothing but comply. Shortly afterwards Potter was shot down in the road. The deputy reported facts in town and an inquest held on the body of Potter. Nothing is known as to who the parties were or the object of the killing. Potter had been arrested and was on his way to be tried for horse stealing.

The widow of M. E. Cushing, of Houston, died this morning.

A special from Laredo says Postmaster Ford was arrested yesterday on a warrant from United States Commissioner Paschal for refusing to deliver a registered package to a man without proper identification.

Fred Gross, son of a banker and a popular young man, died this morning at seven o'clock. He had a very large funeral this afternoon.
The wool market seems considerably disturbed. Local prices are way up, while advices from the coast indicated a decline. The gentlemen interested in the San Antonio & Mexican Border railway are busy looking about the city and the country west preparatory to making out a definite line for the road.

Desperate Duel Between Negroes.
ATLANTA, GA., August 2.—A report comes from Monroe county of a duel between two negroes, Bill Comer and Frank Cheney, at a negro wood-chopping. They quarretled, a challenge passed and was accepted, when they proceeded to settle matters on the spot in accordance with the code, the weapons being pistols. Cheney used a Derringer which missed fire. Comer, with a revolver, lodged a ball in Cheney's thigh. Again Cheney's Derringer failed, and be received another ball in the leg. Trying his Derringer once more without success, he threw it down, and seizing an axe struck at Comer, who warded off the blow and shot Cheney dead at close range. Comer escaped.

Election Fights in Kentucky.
AUGUSTA, KY., August 2.—This town was the scene of much disorder at the election yesterday and many fights occurred during the day. In the evening a fight occurred at the Landing, in which pistols were used and one man known to have been wounded. The marshal met with resistance while endeavoring to make arrests, but managed to secure his prisoners.

United States Mail Robbery in Texas.
GALVESTON, August 2.—A special to the News from Uvalda, in this State, says: "The east-bound stage was robbed at a point four miles west of here last Sunday night. The passengers were not disturbed, but the mails were systematically robbed."

A Captain of Police Murdered.
LEXINGTON, KY., August 2.—Captain C. M. Hendricks, of the police force here, was shot dead yesterday by Charles Steele, a negro saloon-keeper, while endeavoring to arrest him. The murderer has been arrested.

An Escaping Criminal Shot Dead.
DRESDEN, TENN., August 2.—Sunday last Jordan Thompson (colored) cut a white man with a razor and fled. He was pursued by officers, who, on his refusal to surrender, shot him dead.

A Negro Lynched.

DYERSBURGH, TENN., August 2.—Mike Walls (negro) was lynched here yesterday upon his confession of having attempted to assault Mrs. J. F. Childress.

An unfortunate, but apparently well-meaning man named Gallagher, at Santa Fe, undertook to remonstrate with Juan Montera for his unfilial behavior in habitually abusing his mother. Near Mt. Vernon, Ky., on the 18th inst., James Hart shot Andrew Baker dead. They were both drunk, and Hart claims that the shooting was accidental.

Johu McCombe, a prominent Colorado politician shot and probably fatally wounded James McDonald, an actor, at Leadville, Col., on the 17. Cause, misunderstanding in regard to the use of a buggy.

Robert B. Cyphert, a leading citizen of Marion county, Arkansas, was shot by an assassin while standing in his doorway.

A crazy man shot and severely wounded Miss Fannie Walker at Elizabethtown, N. J., on the 17th inst., and then killed himself.

Thos. Meyer, of Rantowles, S. C., crazed by religion, shot his 13-year-old boy as a sacrifice on the 13th. He failed in the attempt to murder two more of his children. The murderous father persuaded his little son to walk ahead of him on the road, and then deliberately shot him down.

A printers' strike at Pittsburgh, Pa., resulted in a tragedy on the 16th inst. One of the displaced men named Michael Corcoran, assaulted a "rat" and was shot dead.

At a saw-mill fifteen miles from Hot Springs, Ark., on the 15th inst., R. L. Justice was shot with a rifle by a man named Gregg, who had also recently killed a negro.

Juan Monterea, of Toas, New Mexico, killed Lem Gallagher with a hoe, for interfering in a fight with his mother. A lynching party swung Mouterea from the court house railing on the same evening.

Geo. L. Larkin, deputy United States marshal, killed his cousin, also named Larkin, at Rogerville, Tenn., on the 15th inst. The deceased had violated the laws and was resisting arrest when shot down.

Clay Wilson, a notorious gambler, was shot dead at Denver, Col., on the 16th, by James Moor, another of the gentry.

At Bedford, Ind., Wm. Brannan was shot by a concealed assassin and instantly killed.

Robert Martin shot his wife and child, a girl three years old, at Newark, N. J., on the 15th inst. The woman was instantly killed and his child mortally wounded.

Freeman Alvoirs, a lunatic, was murdered by Byron L. Day, a fellow unfortunate at Wauwatosa, Milwaukee county, Wis., on the 13th inst.

Two neck-tie sociables on the 13th inst.—one at Denver, Ark., and the other at Weston, Neb. At the former place Emory, a murderer, was taken from jail and hung; and at the latter village Charles Diddell, a negro rapist, had his neck stretched by an angry populace.

Timothy Mahoney, a policeman, was shot dead by burglars at Chicago, on the night of the 12th inst.

Wm. Gordon and Peter Magnus quarrelled at Chicago on the 12th, when Magnus kicked Gordon in the neck, causing instant death.

Patrick Mallory was shot and killed by James McDonough at Cincinnati, on the night of the 12th.

SAM S. JONES and Dell Kribs, both young men, went over the dam at Marshalltown, Iowa, and were drowned.

LUDINGTON, Mich., has been almost destroyed by fire. The entire business portion of the town is swept away. Loss about $200,000.

A PARTY of armed men took possession of the jail at Dover, Pope County, Ark., on the 13th, and hung Cal. Emery, the wife-murderer, whose death sentence Governor Churchill a few weeks since commuted to twenty-one years' imprisonment in the Penitentiary. Emery resisted and was shot in the head. THE jury in the Victoria disaster investigation, at London, Out., have found a verdict censuring the owner, captain, and engineer of the ill-fated vessel. The Government Inspector is also held to blame.

OWING to violations of treaty stipulations existing between the Governments of the United States and Mexico, the Governor of Texas has issued a proclamation with a view of putting a stop to them.

MR. CLIVE HERSEE, a well-known member of the Solden Opera Company, committed suicide by jumping from a bridge into the river near Central City, Colo. His matrimonial relations were unhappy.

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., has been constituted a port of delivery.

A SPECIAL from Winnepeg says war has broken out between the Sioux and Crees. A battle has been fought near the Moody Mountain, in which twenty-eight of the former were killed.

The recent fire at Quebec, according to official reports, destroyed 642 houses, rendering 1,211 families, or 6,028 people, homeless. Two-thirds of these lost their all, and had no insurance.

It is reported that DeLesseps' canal project on the Isthmus of Panama does not progress favorably. Stations have been abandoned, brigades disbanded and many engineers have returned home and workmen have been discharged. The Star and Herald says: "We would like to see a little more accomplished on the isthmus, and a little less blowing in Paris about the business."

The Illinois State Board of Health has issued a circular to the different health authorities of the Northwest inviting them to a conference at Chicago, on June 29, to take into consideration a plan for concert of action, in connection with the National Board of Health, to prevent the introduction into this country and spread of smallpox. The prevalence of small-pox at this time is noteworthy. It is now known to exist at seven points in Illinois, and is mainly owing, it is asserted, to its introduction by immigrants.

NEAR Weston, Platte County, Mo., a negro named Charles Didell assaulted a young lady named Nancy Stillwell, and after a violent struggle, in order to shield himself from the discovery of his crime, cut his victim's throat. He was discovered by two ladies passing by, who gave the alarm. The villain fled, but was pursued and captured by a party of citizens, forced to confess, and was then hanged to a bridge, the brother of the victim adjusting the noose.

SILAS M. WAITE, until recently President of the First National Bank of Brattleboro, Vt., has been found guilty of fraud and embezzlement and sentenced to six years' imprisonment in the House of Correction.

JUAN MONTEREA killed Leon M. Gallagher in Taos County, N. M., and was hanged by the vigilantes.

GEN. R. C. NEWTON, who was sent by the Governor of Arkansas to investigate the troubles in Perry County, has returned and reports everything quiet and the affair greatly exaggerated. He says the civil officers are amply able to enforce the laws, and anticipates no further disturbances.

At Rogers' Mills, Ga., the other day, Mr. and Mrs. John Middleton were drowned while boating.

ROBERT MARTIN, an Englishman, 50 years of age, living in Newark, N. J., shot his wife and child on the 14th. The woman was almost instantly killed. The child, a girl two years and six months old, was wounded in two places, it is thought fatally. Martin was arrested.

MYERS and Brown, the New Madrid (Mo.) murderers, have been sentenced to be hanged on the 15th of July, and Mitebell, as accessory to the crime, has been sentenced to thirty years' in the Penitentiary.

PATRICK Morris and Thomas Regan perished in a fire at Pierrepont's stores, Brooklyn, N. Y., on the 15th. The loss on bonded goods and buildings is estimated at $100,000.

The two stages running between Fayetteville and Alma, Ark., were both robbed on the night of the 15th, near a point where they pass each other, about twenty miles north of Alma. The north-bound stage first came along and was stopped: the robbers, two in number, presenting their revolvers at the head of the driver, compelled him to dismount and have his hands secured, after doing which they blindfolded and bound the passengers, at the same time relieving them of their valuables. The robbers did not get a very heavy return for their labors, only about $35 in cash and a gold watch and chain.

VINCENNES, Ind., Aug. 15.—In the White River bottoms, twenty miles southeast of Vincennes, Lake Mosby, from the ambush of a hedge, fired two rifle balls into the body of Lawson Hewett while the latter was ploughing in his field last Friday afternoon. MEMPHIS, December 20th.—Special from Tupulo Station, Miss., on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, give the following account of a horrible crime committed in the northern portion of Monroe county, Mississippi, last Saturday night. Mr. Brown, a young man raised in the neighborhood, married and built a house near that of his parents. His family consisted of a wife and daughter two years old. On Saturday night two men, giving the names of Metter, called and asked to stay all night. The evening being so disagreeable they were permitted to remain and occupy a bed in the same room with the family, it being the only one where there was a fire. About 11 o'clock flames from the little cottage attracted the neighbors, who found the house so far consumed that nothing could be done toward saving it. It was the impression that the family had absented themselves for the night, but in the debris was found the crisp and charred remains of the little family. Excited indignation took full sway, and an investigation developed the above. Search was at once made for the two men, and it was found that they had separated, one going towards Aberdeen, the other direct to Polo. The posse that went in pursuit of the Aberdeen-bound man were successful, finding him hid in a field six miles from Aberdeen. Last night he was returned to the scene, when he told the following story: "We wanted money. Are the People of Pennsylvania Civilized?
Recently, near the town of Tupelo, in Mississippi, a horrible crime was horribly punished. Two strangers were given shelter for the night by a family, simply out of kindness. The men thus sheltered arose in the night and chloroformed their benefactors robbed them, and then setting the house on fire roasted the insensible inmates alive. The villains were pursued, and one of them caught. He confessed his crime and an infuriated mob burned him alive. Taking this as a text the Norristown (Pa.) Herald preaches a bloody shirt sermon on the barbarism of Mississippi, dragging in the Fort Pillow massacre, the Chisholm murder, the Yazoo homicide and everything it can think of, and it indignantly asks "what kind of courts and juries they must have in a State where the punishment of a man who had acknowledged his guilt of robbery, arson and murder, could not be entrusted to the machinery of the law?"

Last Monday afternoon it was announced that an aged couple living but four miles from Bethlenem, Pennsylvania, had been found brutally murdered, and that a man named Suyder, accused of the deed, was caught by an infuriated mob and hanged to the nearest tree. Later details in the morning papers show that Soyder confessed his crime, and also that the people of the neighborhood approve his lynching. One "respectable "old farmer" told the District Attorney who was criticising the act after it was done that it was all right, and the people did not intend that the lawyers should get any more murderers off on the plea of insanity. In the language of the Norristown Herald we ask "what kind of "courts and juries they must have in a "state where the punishment of a man "who had acknowledged his guilt of "murder could not be intrusted to the "machinery of the law?"

We hope, however, the Herald will not draw too gloomy an inference concerning the barbarism of the State of Pennsylvania from this incident. Of course, a very bad case might be made out, by dwelling on the shameless corruption of its politics, the known purchasability of its legislators, the Pittsburg riot, the Molly Maguire murders and the recent acquittal of a bloody murderer on a trumped up plea of insanity, bringing them all down to this last incident, as the Herald did in discussing the Mississippi tragedy, but the imputation against the majority of the people of the State of Pennsylvania would nevertheless be as unjust as that recently made by the Herald against the people of Mississippi.

A WIFE-MURDERER.

CINCINNATI, O., April 22.—Shortly before midnight to night, John Mooney was arrested for the murder of his wife. The crime was not known to the police nor the public, though the act was committed last Sunday, because her death did not occur until this evening. The Coroner being called in, discovered that the woman died from the effects of a wound inflicted by a batchet. It appears that Mooney has always been passionate and abusive, especially when drunk. Last Sunday he assaulted his wife with a batchet and dealt her a sovereign blow on the left shoulder and neck. Her daughter attempted to interfere, when Mooney throw the hatchet at her and cut her arm fearfully near the shoulder. Mrs. Mooney refused to inform the police of her injuries. She has been janitress of a bank for a number of years. Her husband has no occupation, though he says he is a painter. His age is 37. His wife was 40.

MYSTERIOUS TRIPLE MURDER.

MILWAUKEE, April 22.—Sheriff T. L. Fitzgerald, of Toledo, In., started for home with the jailbreaker Donnis Murphy, who had been in the lockup here since Sunday. The prisoner, on his arrest for stealing a new harness at Toledo three years ago, broke jail and liberated seven other prisoners. A DEFAULTING OFFICIAL.
CHEYESNE, Wyo., April 22.—Col. Gilbert Adams, formerly United States Marshal for Wyoming, defaulted in a large sum while Marshal here, and soon left for parts unknown. with the following jurors, who were selected from a panel of over 200 men:
Noah Smith, A. J. Sutherland, Abraham Brazelton, W. M. Hall, John Schnell, J. L. W. Bennett, Wm. Purdam, J. L. Brandon, Wm. Stevens, Wm. Lynch, H. H. Holt, and S. C. M. Williams. Constable Alex. Caldwell, officer in charge.
A large number of witnesses—about 40, including both sides—were examined, which occupied the time of the Court until 5 o'clock Thursday evening, the 14th, and in two hours afterward (7 o'clock) the argument was opened by the Attorney-General with a two hours' speech. He was followed by Messrs. W. E. Colyar and P. R. Curtis, counsel for the defendants.
Friday morning Capt. T. D. Gregory spoke in behalf of the State, closing just before noon, and the afternoon was consumed by Messrs. John Simmons and Jesse Arledge, defendants' counsel.

Gov. Marks, for the State, made the closing argument. He commenced at 7 o'clock Friday night, and spoke till 9:30, when Judge Williams charged the jury, and the Court adjourned till next morning.

Saturday morning the jury appeared and requested that Judge Williams give further explanation in regard to the charge. The Judge said the only explanation he could make would be to re-read the charge, which he did in his usual articulate style, when the jury retired to their room in the Ballard House. This was about 10 o'clock.

At 1:30 p. m. the jury returned to the Court-room and rendered a verdict: Guilty of murder in the first degree. The counsel for defendants moved for a new hearing, and Court adjourned till Monday morning.

At 9 o'clock Monday morning Court was called. The movement of defendants' counsel for a new hearing was over-ruled. Judge W. then remarked that he was about to perform one of the most solemn duties of his life, and asked the prisoners if they had anything to say before sentence was passed upon them. John Poe raised to his feet and said that they had not been given a fair trial, that prejudice was high against them, that evidence had been produced which was untrue, that he could have produced witnesses whose testimony would have been valuable to them if he had been given time, &c. He then took his seat, and the death sentence was pronounced. Judge Williams said:

"It is the judgment of the Court that you, John Poe and Cicero Poe, be delivered to the Sheriff of Franklin county, to be put and kept in the jail of said county until Friday, the 17th day of June, 1881, and from thence taken by said Sheriff to a gallows within one mile of the Courthouse of Winchester, there to be hanged, each and severally, until you are dead. Said Sheriff shall erect said gallows and said defendants shall pay the costs of this prosecution."

After the sentence was passed, John Poe said, very audibly: "I guess I won't be at that scaffold."

The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, and at 11:30 o'clock Sheriff Turner, with a sufficient guard, left for Nashville with the prisoners, where they will remain until their case is acted upon by the Supreme Court, which meets next December. If the lower Court has erred in the trial they will get a new hearing; if to the contrary, the death sentence will be confirmed and another day be set by that body for their execution.

The Court adjourned about 11 o'clock, and Judge Williams left for Spencer to hold Court for the balance of the week. He will return and hold a special term here next week, commencing on Monday, for the purpose of trying those cases on the felony docket which were not continued.

We do not give the testimony of the witnesses in this trial, because we did not hear it all, other and more important business requiring our attention. It is enough to say, however, that, so far as our knowledge goes, the prisoners were given a fair and impartial trial, and the testimony produced against them corroborated what we printed at the time of their arrest; and, furthermore, the verdict accords, almost universally, with the views of the hundreds of persons who were present during the trial.

LOCALMATTERS.
Murder in a Dance-House.
EX DREW  THE COLORED PROBLEM
Murder in a Dance-House.

POSEY DREW, THE COLORED PROPRIETOR, STABBED TO DEATH FOR REFUSING ADMITTANCE TO A MINOR—ARREST OF THE ALLEGED CRIMINAL—INQUEST TO BE HELD TO-DAY, &C.

Last night about 8 o'clock a difficulty occurred in a negro dance-house at 1807 east Carv street (better known as "Cash Corner"), which resulted in the death by stabbing of Posey Drew (colored), the proprietor of the house. The particulars of the affair, as far as could be ascertained, are as follows: About the hour above named a party consisting of one man and three boys or youths went to the house for the purpose, it is supposed, of attending a dance which was to take place there. Drew objected to one of the boys going in because he was too young, when a controversy ensued between him and the visitors, during which Fannie Chalkley, a mulatto woman who was present, shoved two of the boys out of the door, leaving Drew and the man and the oldest of the youths together. The woman states that she saw the youth hand his companion a knife, and in a few moments heard Drew exclaim "I'm cut to death! Run for the police." The party then ran off. She immediately ran out into the street and commenced to cry "murder," and when she returned she found Drew lying on the floor weltering in blood, and in a few moments he expired.

News of the difficulty was conveyed to the First police-station and Sergeant Howard and Officer Walton went to the spot. At the same time Captain Pleasants telegraphed to Dr. Brock. When the officers arrived it was found that the man was dead, and the Coroner was notified.

From a description given of the parties suspicion was attracted to a man by the name of Charles Bowen as the party who did the cutting, and William Gilham, a youth of about eighteen years, as one of the parties who were present. Githam was found at the Theatre Comique by Sergeant Howard and Officer Walton, and when brought to the station-house was identified by the woman Fannie Chalkley as one of the party whom she shoved out of the door. Bowen subsequently came to the station-house and delivered himself up. He admitted being present during the cutting, but denies that he was one of the party, and says that the fatal blow was struck over his shoulder, but does not know who did it. Bowen bears rather a bad reputation, having served a term in the penitentiary, and also in the chain-gang.

The murdered man was about forty years of age, and, strange as it may seem, was looked upon as a quiet and well-behaved person, notwithstanding the fact that he kept a house that was resorted to by the most degraded of both sexes and color.

Drs. Brock and Taylor made a partial examination of the wound, which had the appearance of being made with a large knife, and found that it had penetrated the cavity of the chest, and that death was caused from internal hemorrhage overwhelming the lungs.

Dr. Taylor will make a post mortem examination of the body this morning at 10 o'clock, and an inquest at 4 P. M.

be the absorbing topic of conversation Sunday and yesterday in the neighborhood of the occurrence, especially among the colored people, with whom the deceased was quite popular, notwithstanding the questionable character of his vocation. After our report closed Saturday night the police were scouring the city in search of persons suspected of being implicated in the crime, and several arrests were made, but, with the exception of Gilliam and Charles Bowen, who were held to await the action of the coroner's jury, in each case the parties satisfied the authorities that they had no connection with the affair, and were released. Considerable interest in the matter was also manifested in Manchester when it became known Sunday that all of the parties suspected of the crime resided in that city.

Coroner Taylor made a post-mortem examination of the remains Sunday morning at 10 o'clock, and ascertained that the wound penetrated the upper part of the right lung about 1½ inches, causing hemorrhage, which produced death in a few minutes. About 4 o'clock in the afternoon the jury, which had been previously gotten together by Deputy High-Constable Whitehead, met at the scene of the murder, and after being sworn in adjourned to the Old-Market Hall to hear the testimony in the case.

Charles Bowen (white) was the first witness examined. The Coroner told him that in view of his connection with this case that he was at liberty to decline answering any question which he thought would criminate him. Bowen stated that he lived on the Midlothian road, just outside the corporate limits of Manchester; that he went to Drew's house Saturday night about 8:15 o'clock in company with his brother John Bowen, Jim Butler, George Binn, and Michael Binn (all white); that he and two of the boys went in the house, leaving two outside. He declined to tell the names of the two who went in with him. Two of the party who went in the house had some words with Drew, who told them they must pay ten cents or go out. They went out, followed by Drew. At the door they met a colored man, and some of the party knocked up against him, or hit him, when Drew shoved the man in the house and closed the door after him, remaining outside with Bowen's party. One of the three who had gone inside handed a pocket-knife to one of the others, with which he stabbed Drew in the breast. Drew had not done anything to provoke a difficulty. Didn't think the stabbing would have been done but for the colored man coming in. Jim Butler had gone off nearly to Seventeenth street when the stabbing was done. He (Bowen) stayed about ten or twenty minutes after the stabbing, the others ran off immediately. Willie Gilliam was not there. Bowen described the person who did the stabbing as a tolerably stout fellow about sixteen years old and black hair, he thought, and left-handed. Did not think his brother was left-handed. Had been told by one of the party what became of the knife, but declined to tell. Saw only one of the boys after the difficulty. The knife was borrowed from Pat. Moore, who lives in Manchester. None of the party were any kin to him except John Bowen, his brother.

Henry Temple (colored) was the next witness. He was inside the house, with the door shut, when the stabbing occurred. Saw some of the parties as they went off, but would not be able to recognize them. He could only tell what happened after the stabbing, which did not differ materially from what we have already published.

Waddy T. Dickinson (white) knew nothing of the cutting; only knew what occurred afterwards.

Fanny Chalkley (colored) testified next. Her statement did not differ very much from that published in the Dispatch of Sunday, except she stated that when the door was opened after the cutting she saw Charles Bowen standing on the sidewalk with his hand raised and a knife in it, as if he intended to strike again. She knew Bowen, and was positive that he had the knife.

Frances Alien (colored) testified, but there was nothing new in her testimony.

Lizzie Kelly (colored) did not know what happened in the house. She was leaning out of her window (which adjoins Drew's house) at the time, and saw Drew come to the door. He stood in the door and told Frances to go and tell Beau Temple to come there. She came back and said she could not find him. He said as soon as he could get some one to attend to his business he would have that fuss stopped. He would get protection. The gentleman standing on the sidewalk said: "We got your protection here; we got your age." About that time Temple came up and started in the door, and whether he struck up against the boy or the boy struck him I don't know; but one of the boys asked him what he was doing. He told him (the boy) to get out of his way and let him get in. Posey told Temple not to have anything to say to the young men; that he could settle it; and Temple went in and Drew pulled the door to with his left hand. After he pulled the door to, one of the boys, who had on a slouched hat, handed Bowen something which looked like a knife, when he (Bowen) raised his right hand and made a motion, and Posey put both hands to his breast, and, staggering up against the door, said, "Halloo murder; I am stabbed to death. Don't let that man get away." Fanny Coleman, who lives in the house with him, ran out, and she and I got there about the same time, and Fanny put her arms around him, Drew crying out, "Hold me up; go for the doctor." She carried him in the house, and got as far as this, when she noticed the blood on him, and asked him who cut him. He then fell to the floor, and she upon him. He lived about ten minutes. When I went to the door Bowen was walking slowly up the street; the other man was on the other side of the street, near Smith's junk-store. The boys I did not see after I came out of my door. Mr. Dickinson was not in the house at that time. Drew was never put into a chair. Charles Bowen was the man who raised his hand with something shining in it. He was dressed in light clothes. I have known Bowen since 1878. I became acquainted with him in the city jail when Captain Tyler was in charge. Drew hallooed "Murder! Go for the doctor," before he was carried into the house.

This concluded all the testimony which the Coroner had been able to get up to that time, and he suggested that the jury adjourn until 4 o'clock yesterday evening, by which time he thought he would be able to get the rest of Bowen's companions, and probably other evidence which would enable the jury to determine who was the guilty party. They were then dismissed until the hour above named.

SECOND SESSION OF THE CORONER'S JURY.

The Coroner's jury reassembled at 4 o'clock P. M. yesterday. James Butler, George Binn, and Michael Binn, three of the boys who were with Charles Bowen at Drew's on the night of the stabbing, having

Jury, after a full and free discussion of all the evidence produced before them, gave as their verdict that Drew came to his death by stabbing at the hands of John Bowen, and that Charles Bowen was accessory thereto.

RIGHTS OF COUNSEL.

When Michael Binn was taken before the jury Mr. S. M. Page, his counsel, objected to his being examined on the ground that he might say something to criminate himself, or that he might make a statement which might be contradicted and thereby used to his injury.

The Coroner stated that counsel were present only by courtesy, and that they had no right to interfere with the proceedings. As will be seen above, he decided to take Binn's evidence.

Judge W. I. Clopton, counsel for Charles Bowen, who was present, in this connection said: "The Coroner's inquest is taken on behalf of the Commonwealth to ascertain, if possible, the very truth of the case, and is necessarily ex parte. No one has the right to interfere with the Coroner and his jury in the discharge of their duty, except that any one who is called to testify has the right to claim that protection which the law gives any one—that is, to refuse to testify if his answer may criminate him, and this he may do in person or by counsel."

Mr. Witt, Commonwealth's Attorney, who was also present, agreed with Judge Clopton.

THE ALLEGED MURDERER.

John Bowen, the alleged murderer, is about nineteen years of age. He worked on Belle Isle, and has lived in Chesterfield just above the Manchester corporate limits for several years. He is tongue-tied and cannot talk plainly; in fact, it is hard to understand him sometimes. Like his brother Charles, he has red hair, and is very much freckled. He lived with his parents in Chesterfield, about five miles from Manchester, on the Broadrock road, several years ago, and it is believed by some that he is concealed in that vicinity now. It is said that he was seen sitting on a fence on the Broadrock road not very far from his father's residence yesterday morning at 9 o'clock. Though not having figured in the courts like his brother, yet he has not borne a good reputation.

CONCLUSION.

Last night the Police Justice bailed the youth Willie Gilliam for his appearance before the Police Court. It is not believed that Gilliam is in any way connected with the affair, but out of abundant caution he was not finally discharged until a full investigation could be had.

James Butler, George Binn, and Michael Binn were remanded to the custody of the police authorities to await the action of the Police Justice.

It is supposed that no further steps will be taken until the arrest of John Bowen.

CIVIL RIGHTS IN VIRGINIA.
Two Negroes Murder a White Man, Beat Others, and with a Crowd of their Friends Parade the Streets.
RICHMOND, VA., February 10.—At a trial in a Justice's Court at Museville, Pottsylvania county, last Saturday, a negro named Sam Wright, who had lost his case, became abusive and attempted violence. Another negro joined him, and seizing sticks of wood killed J. C. Arthur with a single blow and seriously injured two other white men. The negroes then escaped, and, with members of their club, known as the "True Friends Club," paraded the streets, boating drums. The offenders were finally arrested by a posse of twelve armed men and lodged in jail. The citizens could hardly be prevented from lynching them.
sam-wright-museville-1881-02-05.A16: VIOLENCE AND MURDER IN A JUSTICE'S COURT.—At a trial in a justice's court at Museville, Pittsylvania county, Saturday week, a colored man named Sam Wright, who had lost a case, became abusive, and attempted violence to the whites in court. Another colored man became involved in the quarrel, and with a stick of wood struck at every white man he came to. His first victim was J. C. Arthur, whom he felled to the ground, and the next Maj. W. H. Murrell, whose left arm was shattered, and Chris. Kendrick, whose hand was broken in trying to ward off the colored man's blows. Arthur's skull was broken, and after lingering until Sunday morning he died. The colored men made their escape, and went to their club in the neighborhood, known as the "True Friends' Club." The brotherhood resolved not to allow the men to be arrested, and accordingly held an all-night session, marching through the streets part of the time, with the murderer beating a drum at their head. A posse of twelve men, well armed, was organized, and managed to secure the arrest of the culprits without further trouble. The True Friends then planned a scheme to rescue the prisoners on the way to jail, but the officers, getting intimation of this, placed them under a guard of ten men, who, armed with shotguns, rifles and muskets, brought them safely to the county jail. The persons present say it was a most unprovoked and brutal assault, and after the murderer and his accomplice were arrested it was with great difficulty that the enraged citizens could be prevented from lynching them on the spot.

President Garfield will probably return to Washington on Monday or Tuesday, remain there till Saturday, and return to Long Branch on Saturday.
