CHATHAM, VA., March 31.—The execution of the negro Dock Wright, for the murder of Coleman Arthur, took place here to-day. An enclosure sixteen feet high was erected a short distance from the jail, and only the officers of the court, a physician, and representatives of the press, were admitted. The prisoner held a long interview with his mother during the morning, and shortly before leaving the jail was baptized by Rev. W. H. Matthews, of the Presbyterian Church. He declared his innocence, and said that Arthur was killed by his (the prisoner’s) half-brother with an iron poker. At ten minutes past 11 he was

by the officers, under the escort of the Danville Grays, Captain W. T. Hutchings commanding. He displayed the utmost composure throughout, and just after the rope was placed around his neck he was asked by a reporter if he still asserted his innocence, and he answered “I do.” His face was then covered, and a minute later the trap-door fell. His neck was broken, and, with scarcely a struggle, he died in twenty-two minutes. His body was cut down, placed in a coffin, and delivered to his mother.

Threats were made by certain secret societies of which the prisoner was a a member to rescue him to-day, and for this reason the military company was ordered here. But no disturbance of any kind occurred.

STORY OF WRIGHT’S CRIME.

The murder for which Dock was hanged was committed by him at Museville, in this county, on the 5th of February, 1881. During a warrant-trying at that place Dock's grandfather and a white man got to fighting. Dock seeing them from a distance, seized a heavy four-foot stick and ran towards them, striking at the white men present right and left. He broke one man's arm, another's hand, and struck Coleman Arthur, a white man, a blow on the head, from which he died next day. Wright was tried and convicted of murder in the County Court in July last. An appeal was taken to the Supreme Court, and the ruling of the lower court affirmed. The Governor was then petitioned to commute his sentence to imprisonment for life, but refused.

Since his conviction he has been chained to the floor of the jail, but a short time ago he succeeded in cutting his chains loose, and was engaged in trying to cut through the window when he was detected. He was again secured, and two days afterwards he cut off his shackles, knocked the jailer down as he entered, and ran for his life, but was captured before he got out of the jail-yard. A third time he cut his chains off—how no one knows, as no instrument of any kind could be found upon his person. His superstitious colored friends say that the Lord released him.

HIS PROCLAMATION TO THE WORLD.

A short time before he was hanged the condemned man asked for pen and paper, saying that he wished to write his proclamation to the world. He was given writing materials, and left the following remarkable epistle:

TOMAHAWK CREEK,
PITTS. COUNTY, VA.

The year 1863 that I was born on the 28th of October I can remember very well up intil now, but the first year I can remember was very fair in the face; the second year was full of Grace; the third year is woful and sad; the fourth year was merry and glad; the fifth year was loving and giving; the sixth year was work hard for a living; the seventh year for never to want, and I tell you all my advice to the readers both old and young great and small, that have the same road to run that I have run, but my advice to you all my kind readers and likewise list'n'rs watch for that is to come and always take the parents advice matters not what it is.

HEEDED NOT HIS MOTHER AND SWEETHEART.

If I had listened to my mother and sweetheart I would not went to the magistrate's trial, and when a woman tells a man anything it is sure to come to pass.

When any of you get into a difficulty and be put in jail you will see the old jailer come up every morning with his eyes like unto a flame of fire and his face like unto the picture of judgment, and his hands full of a bundle of keys, then his hands are like unto a pair of nail grabs, then your eyes are like unto two balls of fire stuck into a big bank of ashes, seeking for a hiding-place; but when you look around you see the plaster and the iron bars, then all you can do is to lay down and study about your enjoyments which have passed away.

WHERE SABBATHS HAVE NO END.

Farewell to the world, my time is but short to dwell here upon the earth with you all, and may all be prepared to meet me in heavenly Father's kingdom, where congregations never break up and Sabbaths have no end.

Dock Wright's farewell to the world.

Let my execution be a warning for you all, and my young readers keep away from whiskey, for if it had not been for whiskey I would not be in here to-day.

Farewell, my dear old mother; don't you grieve after me, for I am going where my Jesus has gone, for angels are waiting to welcome me home.

A Marietta Man Held on Suspicion.

M'KEESPORT BANDITS.
The Search for the Fugitives Continues-Threats of Lynching.
PITTSBURGH, August 5.—The search for the McKeesport outlaws continues. Two parties answering the description of Nig and Heenan Lightnen were arrested at Hyndman, Pa., to day, and will be brought to this city. The report that the desperadoes had fired on the citizens of Elrod last night for refusing them food was a hoax circulated by the wives and relatives of the murderers to throw their pursuers off the trail and give the fugitives a chance to escape. This gang has been organized for over a year and was known as "the sons of one hundred and one." Their motto, which was full of significance, was "Dead men tell no tales." Ominous talk of lynching and threats are fully expressed at McKeesport that the men will not get to Pittsburgh alive.

JUDGE LYNCH.
A Fiend Attempts to Carry out a Hellish Design, is Foiled and Afterwards Pays the Penalty With his Life.
On last Wednesday night two weeks ago, one of the most diabolical plans was sought to be carried out that has ever been attempted in Lincoln parish in many a day. Mr. A. J. Taylor resides in the Southern part of this parish, about seven miles from Vienna. He has had living with him this year a negro man by the name of Silas Lee who was an ordinary farm hand on the place. Several weeks ago Mr. Taylor went to Texas in order to improve his health, leaving with his family two young men to look after his business and protect his family. On the night above mentioned, some time about the middle or latter part, Mrs. Taylor was aroused from her slumbers by a noise in her room, which she occupied with two or three of her children, among whom was her oldest daughter a girl twelve or fifteen years of age, she arose and lit her lamp for the purpose of ascertaining the cause of the noise which appeared to be at the bed of her daughter and upon approaching the bed she saw and recognized this negro man Silas Lee lying under her daughters bed in a perfectly nude state. Mrs. Taylor screamed several times but, seems without arousing the young men woo were occupying a room remote from hers. Realizing that he was discovered and becoming alarmed the negro crawled from under the bed and ran off. It appears that Mrs. Taylor did not acquaint the young men and the balance of the family with the fact until next morning. No effort was made to arrest him by the young men on the place the next day, for fear he would get away, although he appeared on the place several times during the day and showing by his actions and looks that he was in constant fear of something. On that night (Thursday night) there was a negro wedding in the neighborhood. Silas Lee not being on hand was sent for by some one in the woods near by to come out and help doctor a sick horse; he went and was there met by a crowd and marched off to an old field, tied and literally filled with buckshot and left as dead, supposedly, as he would ever be. But he was not dead yet. After the crowd left him he managed to untie himself and crawl to a negro shanty, not far off, and there remained until Saturday evening, when Dr. Null was sent for. By this time his case was hopeless on account of the severity of his wounds and the time that had elapsed since he was shot that he was without medical aid, one of his arms being literally shattered and his body filled with shot. Saturday night he was again taken out and this time he was dispatched in short order.

He was found the next day about five hundred yards from Mr. A. H. Riter's, in a piece of woods, at which place Coroner C. H. Griffin held an inquest over his body. Thus did he pay the penalty his act so richly deserved. While we do not approve of lynch law as generally applicable to all flagrant violations of criminal law, yet we do approve of it when applied to cases like the present. The chances of escape are two great to allow such a fiend the benefit of a trial by jury and the sooner such characters are taught the necessary consequences of such acts the better it will be for them and the community at large. This villain has been guilty of several attempts before, he was shot in Ouachita parish several years ago and ned from Jackson to Lincoln for fear of punishment for a similar offense to his last attempted, while in Jackson. His end came none too early nor too tragic, considering the heinousness of the crime he was attempting to perpetrate.

Arkansas.
Lynched for Attempt to Commit Rape.
LITTLE ROCK, Feb. 4. Yesterday three white men attempted to commit rape upon Miss Georgia Hamblet, a young and highly respectable lady of Augusta, Ark. ARKANSAS LYNCHING.
Three Men Put to Death for Assaulting a Beautiful Young Lady.
A charming young lady, known quite favorably to many in this city as the younger sister of Mrs. Josie Harry, for whom the popular steamer of that name received its christening, narrowly escaped being a victim to an outrageous assault at Augusta, Arkansas, on Tuesday evening last. The lady is sprightly, vivacious and popular wherever known, and is the daughter of a prominent merchant named Hamblett, at Augusta. While the steamer named in honor of her sister was in course of construction at Pittsburg, a couple of years since, she passed a portion of the summer at that place, where she was a great favorite, and her acquaintances will be happy to learn that no harm resulted to her on the occasion to which the present article refers.

While going from a near neighbor's to her father's residence, shortly after dark on Tuesday, and accompanied by a servant girl, three unknown men suddenly appeared and ordered Miss Hamblett to halt. She ran toward home, was pursued, and when close to the front gate of her father's one of the men caught her arm. The screams of a frightened girl and the approach of a colored man caused the miscreants to desist, and they hastened away, leaving their intended victim uninjured, beyond that sustained by the scare and the shock to her nervous system. The men were pursued, arrested and sent to jail. They proved to be three brothers recently from Missouri, named Tarno. Near midnight a crowd of infuriated citizens took the men from jail, conveyed them across the river, and they were put to death. One account says their bodies were thrown into the river, but this is hardly probable. The feeling against such criminal assaults on females is very strong in Arkansas, and recent numerous outrages has intensified it to such an extent that respectable people will submit no longer to the uncertain results of the laws to render justice, but seek summary vengeance through the aid of Judge Lynch. The Little Rook Gazette of yesterday, had a special dispatch from Augusta, giving the particulars of the crime for which the men were executed.

A RIOTOUS AFFAIR. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. MANITOWOC, Wis., March 19.—Gustave Miller, a Deputy Sheriff of Manitowac County, was shot and dangerously wounded while trying to quell a riot at a Democratic caucus in the Village of Reedsville, in this county, yesterday afternoon. Two brothers, named William and Michael Cohen, were arrested and brought here last night and lodged in jail. The shooting could not be proved against them on their examination to-day, but, as they were engaged in the fight, they were required to find sureties to keep the peace. In this they failed, and were committed to jail. PAGE'S ASSASIN.
AUSTIN, Minn., March 19.—The Grand Jury has found a true indictment against James Riley for shooting Judge Sherman Page in August last. The Judge was fired upon through a window of his study at his home in Austin. The slugs and shot cut his face and breast, inflicting painful but not mortal wounds.

AN INFAMOUS ATTEMPT.

LAS VEGAS, N. M., March 19.—Two attempts have been discovered within the last twenty-four hours to wreck trains on the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fé Railroad. A pilot engine was caught in one place and saved the passenger from going into a bridge. A reward of $500 is offered.

ROBBED BY DESPERADOES.
HENRIETTA, Tex., March 19.—The Gainesville and Henrietta stage was stopped yesterday evening about sundown, near East Belknap, by three masked men, and the driver and passengers robbed. But little of value was found, and the mail was not disturbed.

LYNCHED.
JACKSBORO, Tex., March 19.—The dead body of an unknown man, but supposed to be a horse-thief, was found to-day in Howard Valley, nine miles from Jacksboro, hanging by the neck, and containing nine bullet-holes. The executioners are unknown.

THE KALLOCH TRIAL.

SAN FRANCISCO, Cal., March 19.—In the Kalloch trial arguments commenced to-day, Alexander Campbell opening for the prosecution. Counsel are likely to occupy three or four days with arguments.

A MURDERER ARRESTED.
LAS VEGAS, N. M., March 19.—Marino Lieba, the instigator of the murder of Col. Potter, in New Mexico, has been captured, and is on his way to Albuquerque.

A BAD AFRICAN.

Frank Gilbert, a good-for-nothing negro who has served several terms in the Penitentiary, and who was only last week acquitted of complicity with Jack Orr in the murder of Dick Bross, was yesterday fined $50 by Justice Wallace upon a charge of vagrancy, and in default of payment was sent to the House of Correction. He was arrested by Detectives Ender and Long, who say Gilbert has done nothing since leaving jail but loaf about disreputable resorts on Clark street. He has also been imposing upon people with whom he became acquainted during his stay in the County Jail, and from some of them succeeded in getting small sums on the pretense that it was needed to help some relative out of jail. From Jeffrey Mahoney, colored coachman, he got $10, which was to be added to a fund to be used in defending Prince Albert Jones, the murderer, and on the same flimsy pretext he obtained $5 from the prisoner's mother.

SHOT IN THE HEAD.
A letter to this office from Charlotte, conveys the information that on Monday night of last week, Victor Davidson, a Yorkville colored man now living in that city, was shot in the head, by some parties unknown, receiving a severe wound. The version of the affair as published in the Observer agrees with the letter we received, and is as follows:

Vick Davidson, a colored waiter at Shannonhouse's boarding house, and another colored man, Wm. Wheeler, Monday night, between ten and eleven o'clock, took a walk in the direction of the old Richmond & Danville depot. On approaching the railroad crossing, they passed three young white men, one of whom caught Davidson by the coat, evidently thinking him some one else. Several words were exchanged between Davidson and the other parties, after which the colored men proceeded on their walk. When returning, and at about the same place, the parties met again, and words were again exchanged, and after the negroes had proceeded a short distance, some one of the white crowd fired three pistol shots at Davidson and Wheeler, one shot taking effect in Davidson's forehead, just above, or nearly between, the eyes.

We have not learned the condition of the wounded man.

THE lynching of a young Mexican for rape, the other day, shows a phase of lawlessness probably arising from indignation at the immunity which crime has hitherto enjoyed in this section, and such redress is not absolutely without palliation. Rape and murder are the two most heinous of possible offences. A community which has witnessed the impunity with which murder stalks abroad unpunished is quite apt to rush to the conclusion that rape, also, would pass without adequate penalty. Much as we deprecate such violent invasions of the habits of a civilized community, we really think that lynch law and Vigilance Committees will be the rule, and not the exception, in California henceforth, if some courts and all juries keep up their shameless record of indifference to crimes of violence. If Victor Mirando was only sixteen years of age, disgusting as his offence was, he should not have been
charge of their duties. One thing is certain, viz., the summary vengeance dealt out to Mirando will make rape very very unfashionable in Los Angeles county for years to come, just as a swift and unsparing punishment dealt out to half a dozen murderers in California would soon make wanton and unprovoked homicide a thing of the past in this State. Mr. Forbes, writing from Bodie, the other day, tells a story of lawlessness there which makes one doubt whether all portions of California can claim to be civilized. It is a singular fact that, notwithstanding the numerous unprovoked murders which have been committed in Los Angeles county since the American occupation, the only people who have been hung were swung off by Vigilance Committees. Does this episode of Mirando indicate that our people are prepared to get back to the old summary, if violent and unofficial way, of administering criminal justice?

SUMMARY PUNISHMENT WILMINGTON.
Royal Mail.
The Willows Settlement, on the Cerritos Rancho, near Wilmington, was the scene, on Sunday last, of one of those fearful outrages of which the tramp-ridden sections of the Eastern States have been so prolific of late, but from which Los Angeles county hitherto has been happily exempt. On Sunday Miss Mary Shaw, a young lady between 16 and 17 years of age, accompanied by her sister Mamie and Emma Doyle, all of whom live at the Willows, started for the school house to attend Sunday school. Before they reached their destination a young Californian rode up and, dismounting, caught one of the young girls. She screamed and struggled to release herself, and Miss Shaw, who at first had started to run away, returned to her rescue. By her aid the girl succeeded in breaking the fellow's grasp, leaving in his hand a cuff and a portion of her dress sleeve. Upon the escape of the smaller girl, the Mexican laid hold of Miss Shaw, throwing her violently to the earth and dragging her into the willows by the roadside. The two other girls ran with their utmost speed to the schoolhouse, some distance away, to give the alarm.

Upon their return, Miss Shaw was found in the bushes nearly denuded, her clothing having been cut from her person with a knife. She had suffered a severe bruise and a possible dislocation of the left shoulder, and, it is said that her arm and two ribs were broken. The brute had also ravished her.

Mr. Teal and another young man named Garrison swore out a warrant for the arrest of the perpetrator of the crime and gave immediate pursuit, capturing him, still on horseback, late in the afternoon, somewhere in the vicinity of Wilmington. He proved to be Victor Mirando, about 16 or 17 years old, a resident of Florence, who had been at work some time husking corn for Mr. Bailey on the Cerritos. Mirando at first denied any knowledge of the offense, but afterward confesssed his guilt. As Mr. Teal and his companion were on their way to this city they were surprised by six masked men, who leveled shotguns at them and compelled them to deliver up their prisoner. It was at first thought that the party were friends of Mirando, whose purpose was to rescue him from the law, but it now proves that, after obtaining possession of him, they took him to Mr. Shaw's house, where he was confronted by the injured girl and identified, after which they took him into the bush and hanged him.

The body of Mirando was found yesterday morning by Deputy Sheriff Hayes, of Wilmington, hanging to a willow tree on the ground where the camp meeting was held last summer. An inquest was held by Justice Johnson, the jury bringing in a verdict that deceased came to his death by hanging by persons to the jury unknown. His remains were taken charge of by his step-father.

Miss Shaw, at last accounts, was in a high fever, but it is hoped that she will recover without sustaining serious injury.

Murder Will Out.

SOMERSET, KY., January 11.—Cephus Meece has been arrested for a murder committed in this county eighteen years ago. At that time a man named Willis disappeared, and Meece, Robert Nunnelly and John Gilmore were suspected, but there being no proof they were never tried. Last summer a skeleton was found in a sink-hole, and a negro named Sam Woods said it was Willis, and that he had seen the murder committed. Upon the arrest of Meece Mrs. Meece made a statement that Willis was not murdered, but that a peddler named Phillips was the victim, and that both Willis and Sam Woods assisted in the crime. Willis was here in

September last. Nunnelly and Woods are to be arrested.

Details of the Fire Which Bavaged that Pleasant Village.

Special to the Appeal.]

Some thought it an earthquake, some that a railroad engine had exploded, and many say that they thought of Mother Shipton's prophecy; but, nevertheless, it had the effect of drawing the citizens of our city to the scene of the most terrible conflagration ever seen here. A bill to regulate freight transportation was introduced in the Senate of New York Tuesday. It provides that "every railroad corporation shall give to all parties reasonable and equal terms, facilities and accommodations for the transportation of merchandise, and for terminal handling of the same. All connecting roads shall receive from each road freights, and deliver with equal dispatch as their own is handled from that point. The rates charged shall be no more for short distances than are charged pro rata for long distances."

He was captured by a number of citizens and lynched James Brown, charged with the murder of City Marshal McGuire, a year ago, was taken from the jail at Lake Providence, Louisiana, and hanged by a mob, on Sunday night.

The grocery store of J. P. Andrews & Co., at Climax, Kalamazoo county, Michigan, was destroyed on Monday evening by an explosion of 100 pounds of gunpowder, and 12 persons were injured, three of them perhaps fatally. The explosion took place while the clerk was weighing out a pound of the powder for a customer. The loss of property is estimated at $30,000.

The house of Wellington Moser, in Reading, was destroyed Tuesday night by the explosion of a coal oil lamp. Sallie Rothenberger, aged 14, and an infant perished in the building, and Mary Moser, aged 8 years, was fatally burned. David Maurer, a boarder, was severely burned.
An "ice bridge railway" was laid across the river at Longueil, Quebec, yesterday week, and a large quantity of freight was sent over. In the afternoon an engine broke through and lies in 20 feet of water. The engineer and fireman, hearing the ice crack, jumped off and saved themselves.

The deacons of Bethany Baptist Church in Pulaski county, Kentucky, attempted, on Sunday, to sit in the same pew with women they had taken to the church. This being in violation of the rules, led to a difficulty, and at last there was a fight, in which knives were used, and one man was fatally cut.

A bill was introduced in the Senate of Arkansas, yesterday, establishing freight and passenger rates on the railroads in that State. For passengers the maximum rates allowed from 3 to 3⅓ cents per mile.

It is said that four private bankers of Baltimore have recently advanced $15,000 on forged certificates of the Safe Deposit Company, the forger himself pledging the certificates.

Lieutenant Commander Winn, of the naval station at Key West, reports that the yellow fever has entirely disappeared from that city.

Rome Bulletin: "Robert Scanlan, who keeps a bar in South Rome, while carelessly handling a seven-shooter pistol, accidently discharged it, the ball entering the left eye and passing into the brain. Drs. J. B. S. Holmes, Frank Caldwell and Henry Battey were promptly called, and probed for the ball, which, after entering the brain, turned downwards, and up to our latest information had not succeeded in removing it. Young Scanlan is in a most critical condition, and a fatal result is feared."

Macon Telegraph and Messenger: "James S. Rose, of The Rock," Upson county, writes the Southern Cultivator that he sowed fourteen bushels seed oats on a fraction less than two acres of ground and reaped 212½ bushels on the 20th June. He says also that he has raised 13½ bushels oats to the acre, and believes he can make 150. Of course these oats were properly fixed to grow. They were matured with a hundred bushels of cotton seed to the acre and turned under with a scooter. There's no doubt about crops in Georgia, if they are only fixed right."

Auzusta Chronicle and Constitutionalist: "Dr Frank Deems, a worthy son of Rev. Chas. F. Deems, has concluded to settle in Augusta, leaving the enrichments of New York for the rising glories of the Southern Lowell. We welcome him here, and trust that he shall be as pleased with us as we are sure to be with him. Dr. Deems has had a most liberal education and considerable experience in his profession. He is intelligent, studious and thorough. He has been particularly successful in the diseases of infants and children. To a quick mind and a firm hand he adds a noble heart. We predict for him great success, and are sure that, when once well known, he will be so appreciated that our people will never allow him to leave them."

Cuthbert Enterprise: "Yesterday afternoon, about 4 o'clock, a crowd of mules extending a good part of the way round the court house enclosure was observed, and a crowd soon gathered. On inquiry we learned that the mules belonged to Mr. A. J. Moye's different plantations, and had been brought in that an award might be made to the tenants who had kept their stock in the best condition. After examination the prizes were awarded—$5 for best, $5 for the second, $2 for the third, $1 for the fourth, 50 cents for the fifth. Three tubs were given to the three having mules in the poorest condition. Mr. Joseph T. Kiddoo made the presentation speeches. It strikes us as being a good plan to get mules well cared for."

Albany Railroad, writes this to the Albany News and Advertiser: "Engineer John Green, the 'old reliable,' performed a skillful, and, at the same time, a heroic deed on Saturday last, July 3d. As his train was approaching the trestle just below Dixonia, Green's watchful eye discovered that it was on fire, and at the same time he espied a negro look out from under it. He, quick as thought, blew on brakes and reversed his engine, jumped off, and, in simple parlance, made for that negro. He succeeded in catching and holding him until assistance from the rear of the train arrived. The negro was bound and turned over to the proper authorities. The train stopped before reaching the trestle. It had been on fire but a short while, and had done no material damage."

A LaGrange correspondent of the Columbus Times writes: "Reliable news reached this city this afternoon that is most horrible in the extreme. Last Tuesday a week ago, a white man by the name of Waldroup, living in Heard county, committed a fiendish outrage upon the person of a most respectable white lady, several miles west of Franklin, the county site of Heard. After satisfying his hellish purpose, the villain then cut his victim's throat from ear to ear, and made his escape. However, he was caught and taken to Franklin yesterday, and placed in jail. This morning early the jail was visited by about sixty men, and Waldroup demanded by the mob. He was taken out and carried to the spot where he committed the deed, and chained to a stake and burned alive."

Walton Vidette: "There resides at Centrville, in this county, a very old and decrepit man, by the name of William Lenox, whose life has been shadowed by a remarkable and sad experience. His son Joel, left his home in this county to enter the Confederate army at the beginning of the war, survived all its hardships, and returned to his former home, to find that all his family were dead, except his father, whose whereabouts could not be ascertained. Nor have father and son ever met since their sad parting so many years ago. The son was last seen at Covington, Ga., in 1866 or 1867. The father, after residing in Cobb county for a number of years, has returned to Walton, where he, weighed down with the infirmities of his three score and ten years, makes a scanty living by the sweat of his brow. Any information as to the whereabouts of Joel Lenox will be thankfully received by his father, William Lenox, who may be addressed at Powder Springs, Paulding county, Ga."

Macon Telegraph and Messenger: “On Wednesday last, copying from the New York Commercial and Financial Chronicle, we presented the grand result of the cotton culture of the State of Georgia for the past eleven crops. Six million six hundred and forty six thousand bales of cotton at forty dollars a bale—say $265,810,000, or an average of $24,176,963 per year. What became of this enormous sum of money is not problematical. Any man, by taking his pencil and setting down the probable cost of the corn, meat, dry goods, hay, flour, guano and tobacco brought to this country, will easily foot up an excess of five to ten millions a year during every year of this cropping, and have not one cent to pay for the rice, sugar, syrup, horses, chickens, sewing machines, farming tools, cheese, and all manner of fancy groceries, liquors, wines and cigars, and forty thousand other things poured into Georgia in a continual stream from January to December. The very buckets, tubs, brooms, axehandles, well chains, house and kitchen furniture, paper, knives and pencils, brought to Georgia from the North, would amount to millions, so that, with little thought and ciphering, one is bound to wonder, not what has become of our cotton money, but how we manage to keep going at all with so inadequate a sum as we produce.”

Special to the Courier-Journal from Atlanta on the 29th of June: Mrs. Mitchell, the wife of a respectable citizen of Randolph county, Ala., was found on the roadside between her home and a neighbor's dead, with her throat cut. She had been ravished after a fearful struggle. Imprints of teeth were found in a number of places on her body, showing that the ravisher had lost one front tooth. A man named Waldran, who was known to have been in that vicinity, and he having one tooth out, directed suspicion to him. The trail was followed by blood hounds, and Waldran was captured near Hopkinsville, in this State, and lodged in jail last Saturday night. He confessed to the murder, saying he thought she was a woman who had testified against him in a criminal case, but denied that he had outraged her. Mrs. Mitchell had been married only a few months, and had many friends. She was about 19 years of age. Monday night one hundred armed men took Waldran from the jail and started for the scene of his crime, with the intention of burning him alive. A telegram from there to day states that Waldran was hanged to the tree at the foot of which his victim was found dead. Waldran was only 23 years of age and had five living wives.

ATLANTA, Ga., July 11.—Details of a horrible crime and the awful punishment of the perpetrator come from Newman, forty miles south of this city, on the Montgomery and West Point Railroad. On June 29 Mr. Mitchell found the dead body of his wife, a young and lovely bride of three months, on the roadside, between his home and that of a neighbor. Her throat was cut from ear and there was evidence that a terrible outrage had also been committed. For fifty yards the ground was disturbed, showing the valiant struggle of the unfortunate woman against her murderer. In addition to other bruises on her body she was bitten in many places, the impress of the teeth disclosing the clew that one of them was absent. This led the suspicion to one Waldrop, who was known to be minus a tooth, and who had also been seen in the vicinity of the murder shortly before the deed was committed. Blood hounds were taken to the spot where the tragedy was enacted and put on the track of the murderer who was traced to Hogantville and captured. When taken his clothes were bespattered with blood. Waldrop acknowledged the killing but denied the outrage. The news of the capture and confinement of the murderer, who was taken to Franklin, Ga., spread rapidly through the adjacent counties, and on Monday night, the 4th 100 undisguised men, well armed, entered the town, determined as they said to have the prisoner or destroy the jail. The jailer yielded the keys, when Waldrop was secured and returned to the spot where the shocking crime was committed, which place was reached yesterday, when Waldrop was tied to a stake and roasted alive. It is said that the wretch was saturated with oil before the brand was touched to the brush heap by which he was surrounded, but the report is regarded as sensational, the dispatches not mentioning it. Waldrop was only twenty-three years old, but had five wives living.

The Quitman Free Press has been enlarged, otherwise much improved, and announces Mr. John W. White as local editor.

Mr. Whittle, member from Lowndes county, has introduced a bill in the Legislature requiring traveling doctors to pay fifty dollars for a license in each county which they visit. This may be called a bill to prohibit medical itineracy.

Near Athens the other day a negro went over to a white neighbor's house, and accused two young men of stealing his chickens. A battle began. The negro was struck over the head and otherwise roughly handled, while he hurled a dangerous iron ball at one of the young men, and drawing a pistol shot at both of them, wounding one just above the left eye. The ball glanced off, and nobody was seriously hurt.

The Dade County Gazette says a mulatto of the Furnace stole a horse last week from Mr. James Campbell, was pursued, overtaken in a Baptist Church asleep, arrested, carried before a magistrate, and will probably go round the mountain for about ten years.

Mr. John Abernathy, a farmer, living some ten miles from Cave Spring, cut his throat from ear to ear on Thursday last. He was buried on Friday. Cause—aberration of the mind on account of his crops and other similar causes. He leaves a wife and several children, and was a good citizen.

AWFUL VENGEANCE.
Dealt Out to a Rapist and Murderer.
The Horrible Ponalty a Human Fiend Paid for a Damning Crime.
[Special Dispatch to the Enquirer.]

ATLANTA, GA., July 8.—Last night, in Heard county, near Alabama, occurred one of the most horrible instances of popular indignation on record. Jesse Waldrop was burned to ashes for a crime so horrid that the law's delays could not stand between him and vengeance.

Three months ago, in Randolph county, Alabama, Dr. John Mitchell, a prominent young physician, married Carrie Knight, famed for her beauty and accomplishments. On the 29th of June, in the joy of their honeymoon, Dr. Mitchell was walking up the road near his country home, when he beheld what almost paralyzed him with horror. His lovely wife lay before him a ghastly corpse. Her throat was cut from ear to ear, and her body wrs torn with the fearful clutches of her murderer. It was discovered that she had been raped and murdered. The neighborhood was at once aflame with excitement, and search for the guilty wretch was begun. Jesse Waldrop had not long been in the county, but there had followed him rumors of his bad character. He was seen on the road near where the corpse was found on the day of the murder. In the death-struggle the murderer had bitten his victim severely on the cheek and left signs that one of his front teeth was out. Waldrop had this peculiarity. With these evidences search for him was begun at once, and it was found that he had fled. Trained bloodhounds were obtained, and from the scene of the murder they tracked him several miles into Georgia. Here the pursuing party heard that Waldrop had passed. Gradually tracing him, they arrived at Newnan, thirty miles from Atlanta, where a ferryman described a man who had crossed the night before, and the pursuers knew that Waldrop could not be far away. At midnight on the 3d the party reached a house where they learned a man calling himself Owen had stopped. They demanded to be shown to his room, and, rapping on it, Waldrop came out. He was seized, and after a desperate resistance bound. He denied all knowledge of the crime, and was taken to jail, though the fury of some of the crowd demanded his instant death.

Late yesterday afternoon the scene of the murder was reached. Nothing was done rashly, but preparations were made for the execution with ghastly coolness. Waldrop was firmly tied and bound with wire to a stake driven on the spot where his victim was found, when for the first time his dogged courage failed. He pleaded piteously, not for life, but only to be allowed to die by the gallows or bullet; but he cried to men of stone and at midnight one of the relatives of the unfortunate woman applied the torch to the pine which saturated with oil had been piled around him. His screams rang out on the quiet country air, and the flames lit up the scene with lurid glare. The death struggles were horrid, but not a man stirred. Standing in a circle around the human sacrifice, they looked with stolid indifference on the horrid expiation of the crime. From first to last the officers made no effort to save the prisoner for a legal doom. If they had it would have been futile, for popular passion was fairly frenzied. Waldrop was twenty-three years old, and a man of good address.

Swift and Terrible Retribution. On the 90th of June in Rendelph
On the 29th of June, in Randolph county Georgia, Mrs. Carrie Mitchell, a beautiful and accomplished young married lady, was found by her husband in the road near their home with her throat cut from ear to ear and her person otherwise brutally abused. Suspicion pointed strongly to one Jas. Waldrop, a notorious and desperate character who was seen in the neighborhood that morning, and a party of determined men immediately started on the track of the scoundrel and followed him up so successfully that they captured him near Newman Ala., on the night of the 3d, inst. The guilty wretch fought desperately but was finally secured, finding all hope of escape gone he made a full confession, giving all the horrible details of his assault on the poor innocent victim, her resistance, his brutal passion, the murder and his accomplishing his hellish purpose when his victim was in the throes of death. The indignant and horror-struck hearers took him back to the scene of his crime and binding him to a stake with wire, piled pine knots, saturated with oil, around him and burned him to death and his body to ashes. Who shall say his punishment was not just?

Accusation by a Dying Murderer.
ATLANTA, (Ga.), July 19.—It has transpired that, as Jesse Waldrop was lynched for the murder of Mrs. Al. Mitchell, he called to him Hal Mitchell, in the same county, who was not living with his wife at the time, and said: "Hal, you know you promised to give me $75, and you have caused me to lose my sweet life. I am going to die in a few minutes. I don't fear death as much as you ought to fear the falsehoods you have told to cause my death. I was to kill Mrs. Hal Mitchell, and I mistook the name for Mrs. Al. Mitchell. You promised me $75 if I would commit the horrid deed, and you promised you would give me $25 more if I killed an old man as you intended. I killed Mrs. Mitchell by mistake, supposing she was the woman who swore against me, and whom you wanted me to kill. I have mistaken my victim, but I go to my God with this confession on my lips."

New Iberia Sugar Bowl: Last Monday our town was a scene of great excitement in the vicinity of Justice Langlois' office when it was learned that Constable J. M. Senac had shot and instantly killed a colored man named Jeff Hill, while on trial for beating his wife last Sunday. The facts obtained by us are as follows: During the trial of the case, Hill grew indignant over the statement made to the court by his wife and attempted a second assault upon her; refusing to obey the judge's summons to keep her quiet, Constable Senac was ordered to take him to jail. Hill was persistent in resisting the officer and, finally, making a motion as if to draw a weapon, Mr. Senac drew his revolver and fired, killing him almost instantly. Mr. Senac immediately gave himself up to the authorities and remained in jail until yesterday when he was brought up before Judge Fontelieu for preliminary examination, and admitted to bail in the sum of $500.

During Monday and Tuesday it was rumored that some negroes intended taking Senac from jail and lynching him, but a strong guard was placed around the jail and no attempt was made.

Shreveport Times: For several weeks the police have been on the alert for a negro man named Willian Green, who is wanted for larceny. Last evening between 6 and 7 o'clock Policeman Wimbish got on Green's track and soon discovered him in a store near the ferry landing. The negro saw the officer approaching, broke and ran toward Jones' saw mill, and was distancing Wimbish so badly that he called to several to stop the thief, when Mr. Wiley Downs rushed out from Jones' mill and captured Green and held him until the officer arrived when he turned the prisoner over to him. No sooner was Green, who is a man of superior physical strength, in the custody of Mr. Wimbish, than he grabbed him by the throat, began chocking him and swearing at the top of his voice that there were not policemen enough in town to arrest him. Mr. Wimbish managed to get his pistol out and dealt the negro several blows over the head before he could be induced to relax his hold. Mr. Downs again came to the assistance of the officer and also another gentleman and between the three they soon secured the desperate negro. Meantime a large number of negroes had assembled and violently opposed the officer and Mr. Downs and threatened to rescue Green at all hazards, and only for the coolness and determination displayed by the white men the negroes doubtless would have carried their threats into execution. Last night Chief Austin instructed the force to arrest the ring leaders and lock them up.
